p: The system requirements review passed with four actions, and HEARTH's baseline was set at three hundred and ninety six requirements.
Helen said it was the first set she'd read that sounded like it had met a crew.
Wes had three changes waiting for Friday's board: a hatch handle on both sides, seat track down both sides of the aisle, and every harness run overhead.
Then Nadia found his revision C hatch drawing on the plotter, dated before anyone decided the changes, with all three drawn in and the aisle eleven centimeters narrower than the tape.
Her father had texted that she'd missed Sunday with Callie, so Sunday at noon is in her calendar now with an alarm on it.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He drew his changes before the board decided them.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model. He presented the trace at the review.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead, now planning how to check every line.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She shook Nadia's hand after the review.
Odette. Safety engineer. She asked what has to break for the hatch to open.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She asked for sixty seconds, knowing better.
New in this chapter: Ansel Teague.
Chapter four. Shape of the System.

Revision C had come off Wes's plotter three days before the requirements review. On Friday of week six Nadia took it to his desk at a quarter past eight, before the board met, before she could talk herself out of it. She'd practiced the first sentence in the hallway. You drew this before anyone decided it.

Wes's desk was the one by the windows. He had a breakfast burrito going and the structures schedule up on both screens. His paperweight was a test coupon from a pressure vessel, bent in half on purpose.
She spread the sheet over his keyboard. This is really clean work, she said.
So that was what came out instead.
It's a hatch, Wes said. I've drawn forty.
The aisle's eleven centimeters narrower than the tape.
Seat track down both sides. Crew needs somewhere to clip stuff that isn't the floor. He found note eight with a finger that had salsa on it. Every cargo module had it.
Cargo didn't sleep in there. She didn't say that either. She said, Can we talk about the aisle?

We're talking. There was a photo pinned over his desk of the 2019 cargo module in the test cell, the one that leaked at the hatch seal. Wes had found that leak himself. Everybody at FRO knew the story, mostly from Wes. He'd been right about almost everything since she got here, which made this harder.
Her stomach did its usual thing. The next word was supposed to be no. She was already shopping for a nicer one.
Wes's three change requests were first on the board's agenda at ten. The drawing had already answered all three.
Structures releases the frame drawings in two weeks, Wes said, or the long lead aluminum slips a month. Amara will tell you the same.
Revision C showed where everything went. The sentence she'd practiced was still out in the hallway.

She says it in one breath, which isn't how she rehearsed it. Revision C is a candidate, not the architecture, until they know what the module has to do, and the frames that don't touch the aisle can go now. Wes looks at her for a while. Which frames. She has them circled already. He releases six of nine that afternoon and writes HOLD on the other three in block letters. Two weeks, he says. Then I want my aisle back.

Functional and physical architecture develop together, but the functions come first so the elements answer real needs. Treating a drawing as one candidate keeps it honest, and freeing the parts no open function depends on protects the schedule.

Colleen volunteered Saturdays at the air museum at old Lowry, and she met Nadia beside a jet trainer with an access panel off its side. Behind the panel ran a bundle of wire as thick as a wrist, every wire tagged at both ends.
Everybody photographs the cockpit, she said. This is the airplane.
Wes drew a good airplane, Colleen said. Now ask him what it's for, one function at a time.
Two different crews built the front and back of this airplane, Colleen said. The wire works because they agreed on the plug before either one built anything.
Colleen climbed into the front seat and pointed at the gauges. Each one showed one thing to the person who needed it.
This jet was never the system, Colleen said, and patted the panel closed. The system was the jet, the tankers, the radar, the tower, and a thousand people who didn't work for my wing.
Before she left, Colleen asked about Jun.
Somebody put your name forward once, she said. Your turn.

Sunday at noon the alarm she'd set went off, and she made the call she'd promised. Monday she and Jun took the big conference room, the one with the old lighting diagram still ghosted under the whiteboard.

Jun had started a function list over the weekend. It was long, and it read like a parts catalog: air rack functions, thermal functions, power functions. That's how Wes splits up the work, he said. So that's how I split up the functions.

Nadia has him start over from what HEARTH must do, with no hardware in it. They put five verbs at the top: keep the crew alive, protect them from hazards, house them, connect to the station, support the module for fifteen years. By Wednesday "protect from hazards" has a branch that runs detect fire, warn the crew, stop the air moving, put it out. None of the boxes has a part number. Jun keeps reaching for one and stopping.

A functional architecture describes what the system does and the flows between functions, without naming hardware. Organizing it by subsystem bakes in the physical answer and hides functions no subsystem owns.
By Thursday Jun had turned the functions and the subsystems into an N-squared diagram, printed on a plotter sheet that covered the conference table.

Jun's first N-squared draft. Eight elements run down the diagonal, from structure to Halo Station, and each row shows what that element sends. The air rack's row sends heat to thermal, status to avionics, and cabin air to crew systems. Twenty one of the fifty six cells are marked.

Tiago leaned on the table with both hands and tapped the air rack's row. That one's going to be trouble. Every mess I've ever had in a test cell started in a row like that. Wes wanted to know what anybody planned to do with a chessboard.

Twenty one marks become twenty one entries in an interface register, each with two owners and a blank where the definition goes. Only power and thermal have more marks than the air rack, and those two are FRO's own. Tiago circles the air rack's row in pencil and this time doesn't say anything.

An N-squared diagram finds interfaces systematically: each off-diagonal mark is something one element gives another. Turning marks into managed interfaces, and noticing the most coupled elements, is what makes it worth printing.

The next week Jun moved the architecture into the model. Wes came by while an internal block diagram was on the screen: a block for each subsystem, small squares along their edges, and lines running between the squares.
Ports, Jun said. Where things go in and out. Wes looked at Nadia as if the answer had been a dare.

Nadia tells Jun to keep the internal block diagrams under the block breakdown and type every port. He does: 120 volts DC, coolant at a set flow and temperature, a data link, cabin air. When he joins two ports of different types, the line turns red. He does it once on purpose so Wes can see. Huh, Wes says. It argues back.

In SysML a block definition diagram shows what the system is made of, and an internal block diagram shows how the parts connect through ports, with typed flows. Typed ports let the model catch a mismatched interface before the hardware does.
By the end of week seven they were allocating. Each function went to the element that would perform it, and each got a verification point: the place Tiago would prove it worked.

Detect fire went to the fire detection and suppression subsystem. Tiago asked where he should verify it. Nadia picked the cabin smoke sensor in the main air return above the galley. Galleys were where fires started. Helen's had. And all of the cabin's air came back there to the fans. Tiago could hold a calibrated smoke source under it and watch it alarm. It was testable, and it would pass. In the verification point column she typed cabin smoke sensor, verified by test, and they moved to the next row.
The next row was egress. Hatch, Wes said from the doorway. Hatch is structure. Give it to me.

Nadia gives Wes the hatch, but not the whole function. The egress row becomes four rows, each with a derived requirement traced to the parent. Wes gets the hatch and the aisle. Odette gets the alarm, and crew systems gets the lights. Nadia keeps the whole function, and the parent requirement points at all four.

Allocation assigns functions and requirements to elements. When one function needs several elements, each gets a derived requirement traced to the parent, and somebody still owns the function end to end.

Halo wanted an architecture walkthrough in week eight. Helen wanted to see how a crew moved through the module. The observer from OCSC, the federal office that audits human rating, wanted the hazard controls. Halo's station integrators wanted interfaces. Tiago wanted to know where his test ports would be.
Wes had one answer for all of them. Send them revision C. It's all on there.

Nadia builds each group its own view from the one model. Five views, each with its viewpoint written down: crew movement, hazard controls, station interfaces, test access, and a structural view for Wes, which he didn't ask for and reads first. They all come from one model, so when the hatch moves, it moves in all five.

Under the architecture description standard, ISO 42010, stakeholders have concerns, a viewpoint sets out how to build a view that frames them, and a view applies it to this system. Views drawn from one model stay consistent.
Halo's interface working group would meet for the first time at the end of week eight, and Amara wanted FRO's interface list presented. You present it, she told Nadia. Jun can run the slides.

Jun had built every line of that list. He'd presented the trace at the SRR, from notes, to people who'd already read it. He'd never had to answer a customer who hadn't. He was already nodding at Amara.

In the hallway afterward he caught up with Nadia. I'd rather run the slides, he said, too fast. Honestly. You know the room. He had the list printed and folded in his back pocket, gone soft at the creases from being opened and closed.

Nadia asks Jun to present it himself, with her in the chair beside him. They rehearse it twice on Thursday. The second time, Jun stops reading the slides. Afterward they open the competency framework Colleen sent, and Jun picks two to work on, interfaces and communication. He rates himself a supervised practitioner on both. Nadia tells him he's underselling the first one.

Human resource management develops people's competencies on the project, not just assigns them. A supported stretch, prepared and backed up, and a plan against a competency framework grow the person and the program.

Halo's station integration lead opened the working group with one slide. HEARTH was a small box on it, one of six: the core module, the power and radiator truss, the robotic arm, a lab module another company was building, the visiting crew vehicles, and the ground. Each box had a different owner and a different contract.
The lead said Halo didn't build any of them. Halo owned the station. Wes leaned over to Nadia. Then who's in charge of ours?

At the break a man on the video wall asked for her by name. He was in a dim room with three screens behind him and a headset pushed down around his neck. Ansel Teague flew the station's robotic arm, for the company that owned it, under contract to Halo. He'd flown arms for nineteen years, most of them on the old station, and he'd be the one holding HEARTH for its last ten meters. He had FRO's interface list up on one of his screens, open to one row: grapple fixture, HEARTH to arm.

Halo moved your berthing this week, he said. Not your fault. A crew vehicle needs that port, so you go later, on a pass where I finish in the dark. Your row says the target on your fixture gets lit by the sun. On the new pass it gets lit by me. My lights bounce off whatever shiny thing you put next to it, and then my camera's looking at glare.
Nadia asked if Halo could move it back.

He smiled a little, the way people do at a question they've heard before. You build the can. I fly the arm. The station decides when. You don't get a vote, and neither do I. He let that sit. So give me something I can see. If I can't see it, I hold your module a meter off the port while three companies argue, and there are people on the other side of that wall.

Nobody had broken anything. The schedule was Halo's. The camera and its lights belonged to Ansel's company. The polished fitting beside the target was FRO's. Each piece was fine on its own. Put together, they were one man at a console trying to find a target in the dark, with HEARTH on the end of his arm.

Nadia writes it at the top of the interface list: FRO owns HEARTH, Halo owns the station's rules and how the station behaves as a whole, and disagreements go to the working group in writing. The integration lead reads it and asks if Halo can borrow the sentence.

In a system of systems, each constituent keeps its own owner and management. The SoS authority sets the shared rules and owns the behavior that only exists across constituents. Know where your authority ends.

At the start of week nine Halo issued a station change. Every module would use the station's caution and warning tones and the station's panel, so a crew member heard one alarm language wherever they were. HEARTH's own alarm, which Helen had chosen to be heard in every quarter, was out.
Odette brought the page to Nadia's desk. One alarm language in every module. That's the right rule, she said. We picked ours so you'd hear it through a curtain, though. I want theirs to do the same.

Nadia takes the station's alarm and asks for one proof: it has to be heard in every bunk. Jun traces the change: the alarm function, two interfaces and the audibility requirement. The station tones run a little quieter than HEARTH's. Nadia writes it up, and Halo agrees to a louder speaker in HEARTH inside the station's rules. Helen signs off on the speaker herself.

Station-wide behavior belongs to the SoS authority, so HEARTH follows the shared rule. As a constituent, its job is to assess the impact on its own requirements and settle conflicts formally, not ignore the rule or quietly lose a need.

Tiago caught Nadia in the high bay with a draft test procedure in one hand. Every number in here I typed from the requirements PDF. If one changes, I won't know. Wes's CAD won't know either. The model knows, and that's it.

Jun had ideas about that, and he had them at length. His roommate wrote discharge forecasting software at Halcyon AI, across town, and Jun liked to point out that his own model only had to predict a hatch.

Jun and Tiago wire up the first links in a week. Each test step points to the requirement it checks, and each requirement to the model element and the drawing where it lives. Wes changes a hatch dimension on Thursday. By Friday two of Tiago's test steps are flagged. Okay, he says. That's worth something.

A digital thread connects authoritative data across the life cycle, so a change can be followed to everything it touches. Starting with the riskiest links gets value early without trying to connect everything at once.

Tamarack's proposal gave one number for the heat the air rack would dump into HEARTH's coolant loop. Jun wanted to know whether the loop could take it in every mode the crew would use. Amara wanted the answer by Friday.
Use their number, she said. It's in a signed proposal. Tiago, passing with a cart, said thermal vacuum testing would settle it for sure in about two years.

Jun builds a heat balance for each mode in two days: sleep, nominal, exercise, and a hot orbit. The loop holds in all of them except exercise in a hot orbit, where it's tight. At the top of the page he writes: rack heat from Tamarack proposal, not design data. Nadia circles that line.
System analysis gives decision makers data they can trust: the right question, detail matched to the decision, assumptions and uncertainty stated. Its results feed architecture and design.

Halo sent its interface requirements for the berthing mechanism, station power, data and the radiator loop. The same afternoon Pavel Ruzicka at Tamarack sent an email. Their rack came from the same family they'd flown on the old station, he wrote. It would drop right in, and the details could be sorted out at integration, the way they always had been.

The grapple fixture's section of Halo's package carried a line Ansel had asked for, in plain words: nothing shiny within a meter of the target. The fitting beside the target was Wes's. Stainless, a bracket for the fixture's cover, and Wes had called it out polished, number eight finish, same as every cover bracket on the cargo modules. There was one on his desk holding down a stack of drawings. Nadia set the printout next to it and the overhead lights came right back off it into her eyes, which was more or less the point she'd come down to make.
Wes read the line, then read it again. I polish those so I can see a crack, he said. Bench lamp, tilt it, crack shows. You blast it gray, you're looking at sandpaper.

Ansel's looking at it on his own lights, at night, with people on the other side of the wall, Nadia said. The lights were bolted to the arm next to the camera, she told him, so they pointed wherever it did. She had Ansel's row up on her phone. If he couldn't find the target he'd hold HEARTH a meter off the port while three companies argued about it.
Wes didn't take the phone. So I fly a part I can't inspect so a man I've never met doesn't get glare.
So we berth, she said. You inspect it some other way.

He thought about it long enough that she figured she'd lost. Then he said Penetrant, like he'd been made to eat something. Dye penetrant on every bracket before finishing, then a bead blast after, which was about a day per part, and nobody had a line for it in the schedule. He wrote PENETRANT FIRST, NO BRIGHT FINISH WITHIN ONE METER OF TARGET on the back of her printout in his square capitals and slid it back across the desk. My name goes on that one. The day goes on Amara's. Then he put the bracket in his drawer.
Back at her desk, Jun's list had twenty one interfaces. Eleven had a definition both sides had signed.

Nadia puts the rack's interfaces under signed interface control documents, ICDs, the same as the station's. Halo's integration lead takes the station side. Pavel agrees, sounding a little hurt, to send Tamarack's interface data by the end of the week. Every row on the list has two owners and a due date.

Interface management identifies, defines, controls and verifies interfaces, with both sides agreeing to an ICD that goes under configuration control. Supplier interfaces need it as much as outside ones.
At the end of week eight Jun had presented FRO's interface list to Halo's working group himself. When Halo's lead asked who owned the rack coolant interface, he answered without looking at Nadia.
On Friday Tamarack's interface data arrived.
It came in on the date Jun had asked for, with Pavel's name at the bottom. Jun loaded it into the model that afternoon.
He gave the rack a block in the model, typed its ports from Pavel's data, and connected them to HEARTH's. Three of the four lines turned red.

Jun's interface check on Tamarack's air rack. Power doesn't match: the rack takes 28 volts DC, and HEARTH distributes 120 volts DC. Coolant doesn't match: the rack's quick disconnects are one size smaller than HEARTH's, on the opposite face of the rack. Data doesn't match: the rack's on a fifteen fifty three bus, and HEARTH's avionics are on Ethernet. Only the mounting points match.
Jun looked at the screen and then at her. It doesn't plug in, he said. Not one of the three.

Wes read the three red lines standing up and didn't say drop right in, though she could see him think it. When you call Pavel, he said, I want to be on the line. I've plugged his racks into things before.
Nadia went to the whiteboard. The 133 was still there in its red box. Under it she wrote RACK: POWER, COOLANT, DATA.
She opened a new email to Pavel and wrote the first line before she could think of a kinder one.
